body:
Three Civilizations, Three Environments (lesson): Maya: tropical forests and lowlands; built city-states and farmed the forest; writing system, zero, calendars; many southern cities abandoned in the 800s-900s (drought, war, strain on the land). Aztec (Mexica): an island in Lake Texcoco; chinampas, causeways and canals; Tenochtitlan perhaps over 200,000 people by 1519; tribute empire. Inca: steep Andes mountains; terraces, roads of about 40,000 km, rope bridges, storehouses, quipus, mit'a labor. Alike (examples): both built large states, both reshaped land for farming. Different (examples): the Maya were separate city-states while the Inca were one empire; the Maya wrote with glyphs while the Inca used quipus.

A Soldier Remembers Tenochtitlan (assignment):
Sourcing 1. Bernal Diaz del Castillo, a Spanish soldier with Cortes; written in old age in Guatemala and finished around 1568, nearly fifty years after 1519; published in 1632.
Sourcing 2. He wanted credit for ordinary soldiers, so he may stress their bravery and the city's grandeur (a greater prize makes a greater victory); memories fade or grow over fifty years; he could not speak Nahuatl at first and saw the city as an outsider and an invader.
Context 1. They came with Hernan Cortes, seeking gold, land and conquest for Spain, and arrived in the Valley of Mexico in November 1519.
Context 2. The Spaniards and their Indigenous allies besieged and destroyed much of the city in 1521; Diaz remembers a place that no longer existed, which may make his memories more wondrous or sadder.
Claim. Model: Diaz's account shows Tenochtitlan was a huge, orderly, wealthy city: he says the towers and temples "rising from the water" seemed like "a dream," and soldiers who had seen Rome and Constantinople had never seen a market "so large, so well arranged, and so full of people." The secondary reading confirms the causeways, the island city and a population larger than most European cities. His point of view as a conqueror means he describes the Mexica mostly from the outside and leaves out their own voices and the suffering of the conquest.

The Greatest Achievement (assessment): Any choice can earn full credit. Maya: writing with hundreds of signs, zero, calendars from careful observation of the sky; challenge: recording and predicting time and history. Chinampas and causeways: food for a city of perhaps 200,000 on a lake; Diaz's amazement at the market and the causeway. Inca roads: about 40,000 km across mountains with bridges, runners and storehouses; challenge: ruling an empire about 4,000 km long. A strong counterclaim explains why another achievement was impressive but solved a smaller or different problem.

Scoring tip: in the source analysis, Developing work trusts Diaz completely or rejects him completely; Proficient explains one way his purpose or timing shapes the account; Advanced also uses the secondary reading to show which details others confirm. In the closing quick write, reward any accurate connection to earlier units (for example, chinampas and Mesopotamian irrigation both turned water into a food surplus).
title: Answer key: The Americas Before 1500
